strengths: Originality/significance: CoDiLA offers an intuitive hybrid design—global bidirectional diffusion predictions followed by lightweight, block-local autoregressive decoding—that directly targets a practically important DLM failure mode. Soundness: Theorem 3.2 usefully characterizes the factorization gap through within-block conditional total correlation. Although the manuscript overstates strictness, the non-increase in optimal NELBO with richer block factorization is a relevant theoretical observation.

Empirical results cover HumanEval, MBPP, EvalPlus, and both BigCodeBench splits. On the chosen Dream-Coder-7B setup, CoDiLA generally improves the batch-size-one accuracy–throughput frontier relative to the base decoder and ADJUST.

The soft-versus-top-1 conditioning ablation is practically informative: soft conditioning yields large Pass@1 improvements across block sizes on HumanEval and MBPP. The candidate-scope study also transparently exposes the premature-EOS failure mode.

Presentation is polished and easy to follow, with helpful diagrams and a detailed appendix specifying models, data, optimizer settings, token alignment, software versions, hardware, decoding parameters, and timing methodology.

The paper openly discusses candidate-horizon limitations and accuracy degradation at high parallelism. The ethics statement is generic but adequate for a general-purpose decoding method with no human-subject or sensitive-data study.
weaknesses: The central Theorem 3.3 is not sound. Marginals do not determine a joint distribution: two contexts can have identical marginals but different dependence structures, so one shared function of the marginals cannot recover both joints. The proof's claim that a discrete joint distribution has a unique copula is also false in general. Its per-distribution existence argument is essentially vacuous and is partly conceded by Remark 3.4.

The actual interface is even less sufficient than the theorem assumes: each full vocabulary distribution is compressed to an expected embedding, a non-injective map from a roughly 151k-dimensional simplex to the AR embedding space. Distinct marginals can therefore produce the same conditioning vector.

The top-k support argument does not describe the implemented hard-conditioning ablation. Feeding the top-1 token embedding to an unrestricted AR decoder does not force its outputs to lie in that token's support. Consequently, Table 1 supports the empirical value of soft conditioning but does not confirm Theorem 3.3 as claimed.

Theorem 3.2 establishes only B1 >= BB; the manuscript repeatedly says block modeling “strictly” reduces the irreducible loss, although equality holds when within-block conditional total correlation is zero. Moreover, the theorem concerns an ideal block-factorized model, not necessarily the restricted DLM-marginal/expected-embedding/0.6B-AR architecture that is evaluated.

The claimed preservation of arbitrary-order generation, infilling, self-correction, and other bidirectional DLM capabilities is not experimentally demonstrated. In fact, inference is restricted to the nearest 10 blocks relative to a frontier; expanding that scope from 10 to 50 reduces HumanEval Pass@1 from 51.8% to 42.1%, indicating a material dependence on an order-like heuristic.

The “sub-linear latency” claim is not established asymptotically. Static decoding unmasks one fixed-size block per iteration, requiring approximately L/B sequential denoising iterations for fixed B, while the AR decoder adds B sequential local steps. The paper demonstrates constant-factor GPU speedups at selected lengths, not sub-linear scaling with sequence length.

The evaluation is narrow relative to the broad claims: it uses one 7B DLM, one 0.6B AR model, one coding SFT dataset, one GPU type, batch size one, and a single fixed-seed sample per problem. There are no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, length-scaling experiments, batched-throughput results, memory measurements, natural-language tasks, or tests on other DLM families.

The asserted “new Pareto frontier” omits important context: there is no standard AR-model baseline, and several recent optimized DLM systems discussed in related work are not evaluated. Adding and fine-tuning a 0.6B executor also changes parameter count, memory use, and training cost, but those costs are not quantified.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: no code or trained auxiliary checkpoints are identified, exact benchmark results are mostly available only as plotted points, dynamic-threshold values and complete algorithmic pseudocode are missing, and the identities/seeds of the sampled 300k training examples are unspecified. The custom MBPP extraction protocol further warrants released code and an explicit confirmation that every baseline was reevaluated identically.

Overall, the method is promising and the empirical gains are meaningful, but the invalid central sufficiency theorem, overstated complexity/capability claims, and limited evaluation prevent reliable acceptance in the current form. These issues appear repairable, making this a weak reject rather than a fundamental rejection.

strengths: The core idea is intuitive and potentially useful: a frozen bidirectional diffusion model supplies global predictions while a compact 0.6B autoregressive model restores dependencies within independently generated blocks.

The static experiments cover six established code-generation evaluations—HumanEval, MBPP, their EvalPlus variants, and BigCodeBench Full/Hard—and CoDiLA generally improves the reported batch-size-1 accuracy/throughput frontier over the base Dream-Coder model and ADJUST.

The soft-versus-top-1 ablation is informative: soft conditioning substantially improves Pass@1 for every tested block size on HumanEval and MBPP, supporting the practical value of retaining more distributional information.

The presentation is generally clear and well organized. The paper explains the motivation, architecture, training setup, model and dataset identifiers, hardware, software versions, and several inference hyperparameters.
The work raises no distinctive ethical concern beyond standard code-LLM risks, and the impact statement is proportionate to the contribution.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 3.3 does not establish the claimed sufficiency of the proposed interface. Its proof fixes one joint distribution q and asserts that some parameterization can implement its copula; it does not show that a single shared AR model can recover context-dependent joints when different contexts have identical marginals but different copulas. Remark 3.4 effectively acknowledges this gap.

Soundness: CoDiLA does not actually provide the AR model with the full marginals assumed by Theorem 3.3. It provides expected embeddings e_j=sum_v pi_j(v)E(v). Because the vocabulary dimension greatly exceeds the embedding dimension, this linear projection is generally non-injective, so distinct marginals can yield the same input. The claimed sufficiency therefore does not transfer to the implemented method.

Soundness: Theorem 3.2 concerns an ideal unrestricted block-conditional model p(b_i|x_t), whereas the implemented AR component observes only projected local DLM marginals. Consequently, the theorem does not prove a lower achievable NELBO for CoDiLA. The manuscript also repeatedly says the improvement is strict, although the theorem only gives a nonnegative difference and permits equality when within-block conditional total correlation is zero.

Evidence: The lower training loss in Figure 3 is not sufficient validation of the theoretical or generation claims. Larger autoregressive blocks receive more ground-truth within-block history under teacher forcing, and no likelihood evaluation, exposure-bias analysis, or controlled comparison separates this effect from genuinely improved joint modeling.

Evidence and significance: All results use one diffusion backbone, one auxiliary model, one coding corpus, and batch size one on one GPU. There is no natural-language evaluation, no alternative backbone or executor, and no test of the prominently claimed preservation of infilling, self-correction, backtracking, or arbitrary-order generation.

Evidence: The paper attributes gains to improved coherence but reports no direct coherence, syntax-error, compilation, or failure-type measurements. Functional Pass@1 alone cannot establish the proposed causal explanation.

Evaluation fairness: CoDiLA adds a pretrained 0.6B model and substantial task-domain finetuning, but comparisons do not control for added parameters, data, training compute, memory, or an equally trained AR/hybrid baseline. An ordinary AR baseline is also absent, limiting the practical interpretation of the claimed speed frontier.

The dynamic-parallelism evidence is restricted to HumanEval and MBPP and omits EvalPlus and BigCodeBench. The headline claim of retaining base accuracy at roughly 2x speed is therefore substantially narrower than the paper suggests.

The method relies on a ten-block candidate horizon because wider scopes cause severe premature-EOS failures: HumanEval Pass@1 falls from 51.8% at scope 10 to 42.1% at scope 50. This exposes a material stability limitation and weakens claims of unrestricted global or arbitrary-order decoding.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful implementation details. No code or trained checkpoints are provided; there is no complete decoding pseudocode; exact dynamic thresholds and several training details are missing; and results use one fixed stochastic sample/seed without uncertainty or replication. The modified MBPP extraction protocol also makes comparability dependent on an unreleased implementation.

Presentation contains technical imprecision in the dynamic-unmasking definition: k is described as the number of tokens within a block but is bounded by L/B rather than B. More broadly, several conclusions overstate what the formal results and limited experiments demonstrate.

Overall, the empirical idea has promise, but the central theoretical justification is invalid as applied to the actual interface, and the evaluation is too narrow and insufficiently controlled to support the broad accuracy, coherence, and capability-preservation claims. These are important weaknesses requiring substantial revision rather than minor clarification.

strengths: The core idea is useful and reasonably original: a small local autoregressive decoder uses soft DLM marginals to restore dependencies among tokens generated in parallel, while preserving block-level parallelism and global bidirectional conditioning.

The empirical results support a favorable accuracy-throughput trade-off within the evaluated setting. On six code-generation benchmarks, CoDiLA generally forms a better static-decoding Pareto frontier than Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B and ADJUST; dynamic decoding also approaches sequential accuracy at roughly 2x throughput on HumanEval and MBPP.

The soft-versus-top-1 ablation is informative and shows large accuracy gains from retaining distributional information. The candidate-scope ablation also usefully exposes the premature-EOS failure mode rather than hiding it.

Presentation is clear and technically well organized. Reproducibility is aided by named checkpoints and datasets, optimizer and masking details, benchmark protocols, generation settings, software versions, hardware, precision, and synchronized latency measurement. The work has practical significance for diffusion language-model decoding: it identifies a concrete failure mechanism and provides a lightweight intervention using a 0.6B auxiliary model rather than retraining the 7B backbone.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.3 provides much less support for the method than claimed. Marginals do not identify their joint distribution, and the sufficiency result only says that for each target joint distribution there exists a separately chosen parameterization; it does not establish that one shared AR model can recover context-dependent joints from marginals alone. More seriously, the support-restriction argument assumes the AR decoder may select only from the conditioning distribution's support, whereas the implemented decoder appears free to output any vocabulary token. Thus the theorem does not directly justify the reported soft-versus-hard ablation.

The paper repeatedly says that block modeling "strictly" improves the achievable NELBO, but Theorem 3.2 proves only a non-strict inequality. Equality occurs when tokens within a block are conditionally independent. The empirical loss curves do not repair this overstatement or show that the theoretical optimum is attained.

The evaluation is narrow in model and task coverage: every main result uses one frozen DLM, one auxiliary AR architecture, one GPU type, and code generation. There is no natural-language generation, infilling, editing, or self-correction experiment, despite preservation of these non-causal capabilities being a central motivation.

The broad "new Pareto frontier" claim is based on only the base model and ADJUST under static decoding. Dynamic decoding is compared only with static variants and is reported for just HumanEval and MBPP, not the plus or BigCodeBench evaluations. Comparisons with other recent acceleration approaches discussed in related work are absent.

The paper does not directly measure local coherence, syntax-error rates, or the frequency and types of repaired token dependencies. Consequently, the attribution of accuracy gains specifically to improved local coherence remains indirect.

Results use one fixed seed and a single sampled completion, with no uncertainty estimates or repeated runs. Full numerical data underlying Figures 4 and 5, threshold values, training/sample seeds, code, and an executable implementation are not provided, limiting reliable reproduction.

Limitations are treated only partially. The premature-EOS problem and degradation at large blocks are acknowledged, but the paper lacks a dedicated discussion of dependence on tokenizer compatibility, the restricted candidate horizon, added memory and training costs, benchmark generalization, and failure modes of the marginal-only interface. The ethics discussion is adequate for the method's low incremental risk, though it is generic and does not discuss dataset licensing or risks from generated code.

strengths: The practical idea is intuitive and potentially useful: a frozen bidirectional diffusion model supplies global information while a compact autoregressive model enforces dependencies only within short blocks, preserving more parallelism than full left-to-right verification.

The code-generation evaluation is reasonably broad, covering HumanEval, MBPP, EvalPlus, and both BigCodeBench splits. Under static parallelism, CoDiLA generally provides a better accuracy-throughput tradeoff than Dream-Coder and ADJUST, with especially large reductions in HumanEval extraction/syntax failures.

The paper includes useful ablations on block size, conditioning, auxiliary-model size, candidate scope, multiple-block decoding, batch size, and generation order. Results showing little benefit from increasing the auxiliary model from 0.6B to 4B support the claim that gains are not merely due to a much stronger executor.

Presentation is generally clear, with a helpful decomposition of the method and readable figures. Experimental dependencies, model checkpoints, software versions, hardware, optimization settings, dataset size, and decoding parameters are documented in the appendix.

The infilling experiment provides some evidence that the hybrid construction can still use right context. The impact statement appropriately recognizes general language-model risks, and the work raises no obvious new material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.3, which is central to the justification for soft conditioning, is not valid as stated. Marginals do not determine a joint distribution: different contexts can induce different joints with identical marginals, so an AR model receiving only those marginals cannot generally recover the appropriate joint. The per-distribution existence argument merely allows a different parameterization for each q and does not establish sufficiency for one shared model. Moreover, the actual expected-embedding interface is a low-dimensional, generally non-injective projection of the marginals, making the claimed sufficiency still less applicable.

The top-k argument conflates conditioning information with an output constraint. An unconstrained AR decoder conditioned on truncated marginals can still emit tokens outside the top-k sets; the asserted Cartesian-product support restriction follows only after separately assuming that outputs must be selected from that support. That is not clearly the mechanism evaluated in the ablation, so the theorem does not explain the empirical comparison.

Theorem 3.2 proves a result for an unrestricted block-factorized reverse kernel p(b_{t-1}|x_t), although the method is introduced through a block-factorized predictor p(b_0|x_t) followed by fixed posterior marginalization. The proof does not show that each optimal reverse marginal q(b_{t-1}|x_t) is realizable through the claimed parameterization. It also establishes only a non-increase, not the repeatedly claimed strict decrease: equality occurs whenever within-block conditional total correlation is zero. The training-loss curves from separately trained finite models do not validate an irreducible optimum.

The strongest efficiency claims are insufficiently supported. Figure 5 does not clearly demonstrate preserved baseline accuracy at a full 2x wall-clock speedup across tasks. Infilling reports tokens per denoising step rather than latency or throughput despite adding an AR computation, so it does not establish actual acceleration. Batch-size throughput is also ambiguously defined: both models remain near 70 tokens/s from batch size 1 to 8, suggesting a per-request rather than aggregate metric, yet the result is interpreted as amortizing computation.

The non-causal planning evidence is confounded because the auxiliary AR/verifier is trained on task-specific examples while the reported baseline receives no comparable additional training or capacity. Improvements on graph traversal are only about 0.1–1.0 percentage point and have no uncertainty estimates. On ParallelBench, even K=1 changes substantially, which further suggests effects beyond resolving simultaneous-token incoherence.

All main evaluations use one sample and one fixed seed, with no confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance analysis. This is concerning for small benchmarks such as HumanEval and for sub-percentage-point planning differences. The custom MBPP extraction logic and heuristic EOS penalties introduce additional evaluation choices whose effects are not isolated.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite many implementation details: the displayed code-availability field has no usable link, there is no precise decoding pseudocode, dynamic thresholds and all plotted numerical results are not fully tabulated, and the random training subset/split is not identified. Reproducing the custom extraction, block-selection, fallback, and verifier procedures would therefore require substantial inference.

The significance is currently narrower than the framing suggests. Strong evidence is largely limited to one 7B code DLM and one GPU; there is no language-generation evaluation, no second modern DLM backbone, and no quality-controlled comparison to relevant left-to-right verification methods. The default ten-block scope is tied to a sequential frontier, while the reported Spearman correlations of 0.83–0.92 remain strongly left-to-right, so claims of broadly preserving or enhancing arbitrary-order diffusion behavior are overstated.

strengths: The core engineering idea is intuitive and potentially useful: a lightweight local autoregressive decoder can restore dependencies among tokens generated concurrently by a diffusion language model while retaining block-level parallelism.

The static-parallelism experiments show substantial empirical gains over the same Dream-Coder backbone at matched block sizes. For example, on HumanEval at B=4, reported Pass@1 rises from 24.4% to 51.8%, and Table 1 reports a corresponding reduction in code-extraction failures from 38% to 13%. Results span HumanEval, MBPP, EvalPlus, and BigCodeBench.

The paper includes several useful ablations covering conditioning strategy, AR-model size, candidate scope, multiple-block decoding, batch size, and generation order. It also attempts to test non-causal behavior through infilling and planning tasks rather than evaluating code completion alone.

Presentation is generally clear and visually polished. The motivation, model architecture, and distinction between static, dynamic, and verifier-based decoding are easy to follow. The appendix provides meaningful implementation details, including models, data, optimization, hardware, and decoding settings.
The impact statement is proportionate to an inference-method paper, and I found no unresolved research-ethics issue that independently prevents publication.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 3.3 does not justify the proposed interface. Marginals do not determine a joint distribution: different conditional joints can have identical marginals, so a single shared AR model receiving only those marginals cannot generally recover the appropriate coupling. The proof merely establishes a vacuous per-distribution existential parameterization, which the authors themselves effectively concede in Remark 3.4. It also incorrectly invokes uniqueness of the copula for discrete marginals; Sklar's copula is not unique in the discrete case. Moreover, projecting a vocabulary-sized marginal to one expected embedding is generally non-injective, so even access to the full marginal assumed by the theorem is not preserved by the implemented interface.

Soundness: The paper repeatedly claims that block factorization 'strictly' improves the optimal NELBO, but Theorem 3.2 proves only a non-negative difference. Equality holds whenever tokens within a block are conditionally independent. The ideal unrestricted block model analyzed by this theorem also differs materially from the implemented shared 0.6B AR model conditioned through compressed expected embeddings, so the theoretical optimum does not establish the practical method's behavior.

Experimental evidence: The claimed new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier is supported only against the raw Dream-Coder schedule and ADJUST, despite the related-work section listing several directly relevant adaptive, speculative, and optimized parallel decoders. Dynamic CoDiLA is not compared with a matched dynamic DLM-only baseline, making it impossible to separate gains from the entropy-threshold schedule from gains due to local autoregression.

Experimental evidence: Important reported results are internally inconsistent. The default one-block HumanEval results in Figure 4/Table 4 are 68.9/51.8/29.9 Pass@1 with 18/33/60 TPS for B=2/4/8, whereas Table 6 labels the corresponding one-block HumanEval results as 68.9/55.6/39.3 with 27/47/81 TPS. The latter values closely resemble MBPP results. These discrepancies directly affect the central accuracy-throughput claims.

Evaluation reliability is limited by one fixed-seed, single-sample run and no confidence intervals or repeated-run analysis. Several conclusions depend on differences of only a few benchmark problems. The soft-conditioning ablation is also overstated: Top-5 exceeds soft conditioning for HumanEval at B=4, and Top-3 exceeds it at B=8, contrary to the claim that truncation consistently degrades accuracy or that soft conditioning is strictly optimal.

The non-causal evidence is weaker than presented. Infilling reports tokens per denoising step rather than wall-clock latency, omitting the auxiliary AR cost. The any-order Spearman statistic measures similarity to left-to-right order but does not itself demonstrate preserved capability. ParallelBench uses an AR verifier trained on task examples, while graph-traversal improvements are only 0.1–1.0 percentage points without uncertainty estimates.

Significance and scope: The strongest evaluation uses one diffusion backbone, one auxiliary-model family, and primarily Python code benchmarks. Adding a separately fine-tuned 0.6B model, task-specific training in the planning experiments, and extra memory complicates the efficiency comparison. The manuscript does not adequately discuss these limitations, possible SFT benchmark contamination, or whether the method generalizes to ordinary text and incompatible tokenizers.

Reproducibility is only partial. Many settings are documented, but the promised code footnote contains no URL, the random seed and exact sampled training subset are unspecified, no pseudocode gives the complete decoding procedure, and the conflicting tables prevent reconstruction of the headline measurements. The unusual hard-EOS interface rule and benchmark-specific extraction modification further require released code and outputs for verification.

Originality is moderate rather than high. Combining DLM marginals with an auxiliary AR component is closely related to prior coherence-verification and copula-style approaches; the main novelty is restricting the AR operation to local blocks and using expected-embedding conditioning. That is a plausible practical refinement, but the invalid theoretical framing and incomplete comparisons currently obscure its incremental contribution.

Overall, the empirical idea is promising, but incorrect central theoretical claims, missing matched baselines, inconsistent headline results, and inadequate reproducibility are important weaknesses that prevent acceptance in the present form.

strengths: The central method is practically useful and conceptually clear: a frozen bidirectional DLM supplies global information while a compact, block-local AR model restores dependencies among tokens decoded concurrently. Bounding the AR context preserves meaningful parallelism without forcing globally left-to-right generation.

The empirical evaluation is broad for a systems-oriented decoding paper. It covers HumanEval, MBPP, EvalPlus, both BigCodeBench splits, code infilling, ParallelBench, and graph traversal, and reports synchronized wall-clock throughput on a specified A100 rather than relying only on tokens per iteration.

The static-parallelism results consistently improve the accuracy-throughput trade-off over Dream-Coder and ADJUST on the six coding settings. Dynamic decoding is especially encouraging: the B=4 model approximately preserves sequential-baseline accuracy at greater than 2x throughput on HumanEval and MBPP.

The ablations are informative. They examine conditioning truncation, AR-model size, candidate scope, global versus local selection, multiple-block decoding, generation order, and batch size. The finding that a 0.6B AR model suffices supports the interpretation that gains arise from local coherence rather than simply adding a strong code generator.

The infilling and planning experiments provide useful evidence that the approach retains non-causal functionality rather than merely converting the DLM into an ordinary global AR decoder. The paper is generally well organized, visually clear, and engages appropriately with closely related parallel-decoding methods.

The training and evaluation appendices disclose models, data, optimization settings, masking procedure, decoding hyperparameters, software versions, hardware, and latency measurement. The ethics discussion is brief but proportionate to the incremental, general-purpose capability introduced.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for the actual soft-conditioning interface is overstated. Theorem 3.3 only gives an existential parameterization for one fixed joint distribution; marginals do not identify a copula, so two contexts with identical marginals can require different joint distributions. The paper acknowledges the shared-model problem in Remark 3.4, but still concludes that full marginals are sufficient for reliable retrieval.

More importantly, CoDiLA does not expose the full marginals to the AR model: it exposes their expected embeddings. Because the vocabulary dimension greatly exceeds the embedding dimension, this linear projection is generally non-injective and can map distinct marginals to the same representation. Thus, even the theorem's limited sufficiency statement does not apply to the implemented interface.

The top-k theorem also assumes that AR outputs are restricted to the truncated marginal support, whereas the described auxiliary AR decoder appears free to emit its full vocabulary. Consequently, the support-exclusion argument does not directly explain the top-k ablation. The empirical ablation remains valuable, but it should not be presented as confirmation of the theorem.

The paper repeatedly says block modeling 'strictly' reduces the irreducible NELBO, but Theorem 3.2 establishes only a non-increase; equality holds whenever the relevant within-block conditional total correlation is zero. Moreover, lower observed training loss does not by itself validate a result about the irreducible optimum, particularly when separately trained models are compared.

The strongest empirical claims have limited statistical support. Coding evaluations use one sample and one fixed seed, with no repeated-run variability or significance analysis. Some reported differences are only a few points, and Figure 4's uncertainty markers are not adequately explained. The reported 'syntax error' metric is actually failure of the extraction script to find code, which also captures formatting and conversational-output failures rather than syntax alone.

Generality is constrained by using one principal 7B code DLM, one auxiliary-model family, one fine-tuning corpus, and one GPU type. Dynamic parallelism—the setting supporting the headline claim of preserving accuracy at 2x speed—is shown only on HumanEval and MBPP, not EvalPlus or BigCodeBench. Comparisons also omit several contemporary acceleration methods discussed in related work, so the claimed new Pareto frontier should be scoped to the evaluated baselines and implementation.

Reproducibility is adequate at the configuration level but not yet complete: the manuscript's code-availability footnote contains no usable repository link, several algorithmic details are given only in prose, and the held-out split and single evaluation seed are not identified. A concise limitations section should also discuss dependence on tokenizer alignment, extra fine-tuning and memory costs, fixed block boundaries, benchmark contamination risks, and the restricted hardware/model coverage.
